clinical_knowledge.topic: Primary Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's Thyroiditis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's Thyroiditis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Start Levothyroxine 75 mcg oral daily (taken fasting in morning, separated from iron/calcium supplements by 4 hours), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive fatigue, weight gain, constipation, and cold intolerance for 6 months

Key HPI features: 45F reports 6-month gradual onset of severe fatigue, 18-lb weight gain, chronic constipation, dry coarse skin, and feeling cold all the time. Also reports heavy menstrual bleeding and hair thinning.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 56, BP 110/70, Temp 36.4C. Dry cool skin, non-pitting periorbital puffiness, delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes. Bloods: TSH 34.5 uIU/mL, Free T4 0.4 ng/dL, Anti-TPO antibodies markedly elevated (>600 IU/mL).
Relevant background/PMH: Iron deficiency anemia treated with iron supplements
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's Thyroiditis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Depression without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Very severe symptoms (bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental status) — could indicate myxedema coma.
management_principles: Start Levothyroxine 75 mcg oral daily (taken fasting in morning, separated from iron/calcium supplements by 4 hours)
Recheck TSH and Free T4 in 6 weeks to titrate dose
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize typical systemic signs and symptoms of primary hypothyroidism

Counsel patient on proper administration of levothyroxine and drug interactions
Explain expected timeline for biochemical and clinical improvement

teaching.one_liner: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland causes a gradual slowing of metabolism — fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and coarse skin — treated with lifelong levothyroxine.
red_flags: Very severe symptoms (bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental status) — could indicate myxedema coma

must_ask.say: How many months has this fatigue and weight gain been building up?
Do you feel cold even when others are comfortable?
Have you been more constipated than usual?
Have you noticed your hair thinning or your skin becoming dry?

history.answer: I've been feeling completely exhausted for about six months now, and I've gained weight even though I'm barely eating.
It feels like a deep, heavy sluggishness and whole-body fatigue rather than just feeling drowsy or sleepy.
It crept up on me slowly over the past six months, and it has just gotten steadily worse without any obvious trigger.
It is really interfering with my ability to concentrate at work, and even resting or sleeping through the weekend doesn't recharge me at all.
I feel slow and drained all day long, from the second I wake up until I go to sleep.
I sleep eight to nine hours every night, but I still wake up exhausted. My husband says I don't snore or stop breathing in my sleep.
I feel frustrated because I have no energy to do the things I enjoy, but I'm not depressed and have never thought about ending my life.
I don't get dizzy when I stand up, and my bowel movements are normal brown without any black tarry color or visible blood.
My menstrual bleeding has become noticeably heavier and lasts longer than usual, often going for seven or eight heavy days.
No, I haven't noticed unusual bruises on my arms or legs, and my gums don't bleed when I brush.
I sometimes get a mild pins-and-needles feeling in my fingers, but no numbness or burning in my feet.
I can't stand the cold at all and have to wear thick sweaters indoors, and I've gained about 18 pounds over these past six months.
I have been severely constipated for months, usually only passing hard stools once or twice a week.
My skin has turned very dry, flaky, and rough, and my hair has become coarse and noticeably thinner.
No, I haven't been drinking excessive amounts of water, and I'm not urinating more frequently than usual.
My skin hasn't darkened anywhere, and my appetite is actually lower than usual even though my weight keeps climbing.
My dry skin occasionally feels itchy, but I haven't had any metallic taste or changes in how much urine I pass.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I feel mildly out of breath when walking up a flight of stairs, and my face and ankles have seemed a bit puffy.
Tax season at work was busy, but nothing out of the ordinary, and I drink just one mug of black coffee in the morning.
I was wondering if my metabolism is just slowing down as part of getting older or maybe the start of menopause.
I'm really worried about losing my hair and being stuck with this constant exhaustion that keeps me from functioning.
I'm hoping you can run blood tests on my hormones and see if a thyroid prescription would help fix this.
I was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia about a year ago, which got better after I took iron pills.
I have never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I take ferrous sulfate 325 milligrams once a day in the morning.
I don't have any allergies to medications or foods that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I might have one glass of wine every few weeks at dinner, but that's about it.
I work as an accountant and live with my husband in a house.
My mother had an underactive thyroid and took a daily pill for it, but there is no other major illness in my family.
My last period started two weeks ago, but my cycles have been somewhat irregular and much heavier recently.
My husband had a vasectomy several years ago, so there is no possibility that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate is 56 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, and temperature is 36.4°C.
Alert patient appearing lethargic and slow-moving, with dull facial expression and bilateral non-pitting periorbital puffiness.
Mild conjunctival pallor bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
No cervical lymphadenopathy or axillary lymph nodes palpable.
Diffuse, firm, non-tender thyroid enlargement without palpable nodules or bruits.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory excursion and no adventitious sounds.
Bradycardia with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Generalized cool, dry, and coarse skin with noticeable diffuse hair thinning and brittle texture.
Mild non-pitting edema present over the pretibial areas and ankles bilaterally.
Markedly delayed relaxation phase of the bilateral Achilles and patellar deep tendon reflexes, with normal plantar responses.
